title: Behçet's Disease: A Multisystemic Inflammatory Odyssey
summary: Behçet's Disease is a chronic, relapsing, multisystemic inflammatory vasculitis of unknown etiology, predominantly affecting young adults. Characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, and frequently, vision-threatening ocular inflammation, it presents a complex diagnostic and management challenge for ophthalmologists and rheumatologists alike.

data.title: Behçet's Disease: A Multisystemic Inflammatory Odyssey
data.summary: Behçet's Disease is a chronic, relapsing, multisystemic inflammatory vasculitis of unknown etiology, predominantly affecting young adults. Characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, and frequently, vision-threatening ocular inflammation, it presents a complex diagnostic and management challenge for ophthalmologists and rheumatologists alike.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Behçet's Disease (BD), also known as Behçet's Syndrome, is a chronic, relapsing, multisystemic inflammatory disorder characterized by vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, leading to tissue damage in various organs. While its etiology remains unknown, it is considered an autoimmune disease with a strong genetic predisposition, particularly associated with HLA-B51. The cardinal features include recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, skin lesions, and ocular inflammation. Ocular involvement, particularly posterior segment disease, is a major cause of severe vision loss and blindness.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Risk Factors
content: **Geographic Distribution (Silk Road Disease)**: Highest prevalence along the ancient Silk Road (East Asia, Middle East, Mediterranean basin).
**Prevalence**:
- Turkey: 80-420 cases per 100,000 (highest worldwide)
- Japan: 10-15 cases per 100,000
- Europe/USA: 0.1-7.5 cases per 100,000
**Incidence**: Varies geographically, generally low in Western countries.
**Age of Onset**: Typically young adults, 20-40 years (peak 3rd decade). Rarely seen in children or elderly.
**Gender**: Overall incidence similar, but males tend to have more severe disease, especially ocular involvement, and a worse prognosis in endemic areas.
**Risk Factors**: Genetic predisposition (HLA-B51, MICA, ERAP1 alleles), environmental triggers (e.g., infections like Streptococcus sanguis, Herpes Simplex Virus), smoking.

branches: **Genetic Susceptibility**:
- **HLA-B51**: Strongest genetic association (relative risk ~5-6). Involved in antigen presentation.
- **MICA (MHC class I chain-related gene A)**: Also associated, involved in NK cell activation.
- **ERAP1 (Endoplasmic Reticulum Aminopeptidase 1)**: Modifies peptides presented by HLA-B51.
**Autoimmune Vasculitis**:
- Systemic pan-vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, leading to thrombosis and aneurysms.
- Predominantly T-cell mediated (Th1 and Th17 cells) inflammatory response.
- Neutrophil hyperfunction: Enhanced chemotaxis, phagocytosis, oxidative burst.
- Endothelial dysfunction: Increased adhesion molecule expression (VCAM-1, ICAM-1).
- Pro-inflammatory cytokines: Elevated TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17, IL-21, IL-23.
**Environmental Triggers**:
- Infectious agents (e.g., Streptococcus sanguis, HSV-1) may trigger immune response via molecular mimicry in genetically predisposed individuals.
- Heat shock proteins (HSPs): Cross-reactivity between microbial HSPs and human HSPs may initiate autoimmunity.

branches: **Oral Ulcers** (nearly universal, 98-100%): Recurrent, painful, round/oval with erythematous halo, shallow/deep, on lips, tongue, buccal mucosa, palate, pharynx. Heals in 1-3 weeks, may scar.
**Genital Ulcers** (60-80%): Painful, similar to oral ulcers, on scrotum, penis, labia majora/minora, vagina, perineum. Often scar.
**Skin Lesions** (70-90%):
- Erythema Nodosum-like lesions: Tender red nodules, mainly on legs, but can be anywhere.
- Pseudofolliculitis/Papulopustular lesions: Sterile pustules, acneiform nodules.
- Pathergy Phenomenon: Hyperreactivity of skin to trauma (sterile needle prick).
**Arthritis** (50-60%): Non-erosive, asymmetric, oligoarticular, affecting large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists). Self-limiting.
**Vascular Manifestations** (10-30%):
- Venous thrombosis: DVT, Budd-Chiari syndrome, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, superior/inferior vena cava occlusion.
- Arterial lesions: Aneurysms (pulmonary artery most common), occlusions.
**Central Nervous System (CNS) Involvement** (10-20%, 'Neuro-Behçet's'):
- Parenchymal: Brainstem lesions, meningoencephalitis, pyramidal signs, ataxia, cognitive dysfunction.
- Non-parenchymal: Cerebral venous thrombosis, intracranial hypertension.
**Gastrointestinal (GI) Involvement** (5-15%): Ulcers (ileocecal region most common), abdominal pain, diarrhea, bleeding, perforation.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Features & Examination Findings
content: **Prevalence**: 50-90% of patients, often bilateral.
**Anterior Uveitis (AU)**: Recurrent, non-granulomatous, severe.
- Cells and flare in anterior chamber (AC), keratic precipitates (KPs).
- **Hypopyon**: Classic sign, often transient and shifting (in 1/3 of cases).
- Fibrinous exudates, posterior synechiae, iris nodules.
- Secondary glaucoma, complicated cataract are common.
**Posterior Uveitis (PU)**:
- **Retinal Vasculitis**: Obliterative and non-obliterative. Perivascular sheathing (white cuffing), retinal hemorrhages, exudates, branch retinal artery/vein occlusions.
- **Vitritis**: Inflammatory cells in vitreous.
- **Macular Edema**: Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a major cause of vision loss.
- **Optic Neuropathy**: Optic disc edema, hyperemia, followed by secondary optic atrophy.
- Neuroretinitis.
**Panuveitis**: Coexistence of AU and PU is common.
**Less common ocular findings**: Scleritis, episcleritis, orbital inflammation, extraocular muscle paresis.

**Ocular Examination Findings**: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (AC reaction, KPs, hypopyon, synechiae), fundoscopy (vitreous haze, vasculitis, hemorrhages, CME, optic disc appearance), gonioscopy (anterior synechiae, angle neovascularization).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Clinical Assessment**: Detailed history of recurrent oral/genital ulcers, skin lesions, ocular symptoms, and systemic features.
**2. Ophthalmic Examination**: Full dilated eye exam including slit-lamp, gonioscopy, and indirect ophthalmoscopy to assess for characteristic uveitis, vasculitis, and their complications.

**3. Pathergy Test**: Intradermal sterile needle prick (20-gauge) into the forearm. Positive if a papule or pustule ≥2mm forms within 24-48 hours. Highly specific (90-98%) but sensitivity varies geographically (60-70% in Turkey, lower in Europe/USA).
**4. Laboratory Tests (Non-specific)**:
- **Inflammatory Markers**: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) may be elevated during flares but are non-specific.
- **HLA-B51 Typing**: Performed by PCR. Presence supports diagnosis but is not diagnostic (present in 15-20% of general population). Negative HLA-B51 does not rule out BD.
- **Autoantibody Screening**: ANA, RF, ANCA, anti-dsDNA usually negative (to rule out other autoimmune conditions).
- **Infection Screening**: Syphilis serology (VDRL/RPR, FTA-ABS), TB skin test/IGRA, Lyme serology to rule out masquerade syndromes.
**5. Ocular Imaging**:
- **Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)**: Crucial for evaluating retinal vasculitis (leakage, non-perfusion, vessel occlusion), optic disc leakage, and macular edema.
- **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Detects and quantifies macular edema (CME), epiretinal membranes, and neuroretinal thinning (indicating optic atrophy).
- **Ocular Ultrasound (B-scan)**: Useful in cases of dense vitreous hemorrhage or opacities precluding fundus view to assess for retinal detachment or other posterior segment pathology.
**6. Systemic Imaging (if indicated)**:
- **Brain MRI**: For suspected Neuro-Behçet's (parenchymal lesions, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis).
- **Vascular Imaging (CT/MR Angiography, Doppler Ultrasound)**: For suspected arterial aneurysms or venous thrombosis.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content: There is no universally accepted formal clinical staging system (like TNM for cancer) for Behçet's Disease. However, disease activity can be assessed using tools like the Behçet's Disease Current Activity Form (BDCAF), which quantifies systemic and ocular manifestations over a preceding period. Ocular disease can be graded by severity (e.g., visual acuity, extent of inflammation, presence of complications like vasculitis or optic atrophy) to guide treatment.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Strategy
content: **Goal**: Control inflammation, prevent irreversible organ damage (especially ocular), preserve vision, improve quality of life.
**1. Acute Flare Management (Systemic & Ocular)**:

- **Systemic Corticosteroids**: Oral Prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day, max 60-80 mg/day) for severe flares, tapered gradually. IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day for 3 days) for severe sight-threatening or CNS involvement.
- **Topical Ocular Corticosteroids**: Prednisolone acetate 1% q1h for anterior uveitis.
- **Cycloplegics**: Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to prevent posterior synechiae and reduce pain.
- **Periocular Corticosteroids**: Triamcinolone acetonide (40 mg subtenon or intravitreal) for localized severe inflammation/CME.
**2. Long-Term Immunosuppressive Therapy (Steroid-Sparing Agents)**:
- **First-line (often with tapering steroids)**:

- **Azathioprine (AZA)**: 2-3 mg/kg/day (up to 150-200 mg/day). Often first-choice for chronic ocular disease, particularly for recurrent anterior uveitis and mild posterior involvement. Monitor CBC, LFTs.
- **Cyclosporine A (CsA)**: 2.5-5 mg/kg/day. Highly effective for posterior uveitis and retinal vasculitis, but renal toxicity (monitor creatinine, blood pressure) is a concern.
- **Second-line/Refractory Disease**: Patients with severe sight-threatening posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis, or neurological involvement, or intolerance to AZA/CsA.
- **Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF)**: 1-1.5 g BID. Generally well-tolerated.
- **Methotrexate (MTX)**: 7.5-25 mg/week oral/SC. Less potent for BD uveitis, but useful for joint symptoms.

- **Cyclophosphamide (CYC)**: 0.5-1 g/m² monthly IV pulses for severe, refractory, sight- or life-threatening disease (e.g., severe retinal vasculitis, CNS vasculitis, pulmonary artery aneurysms). Significant side effects (myelosuppression, hemorrhagic cystitis, infertility).
**3. Biologic Agents (for Refractory Disease)**:
- **Anti-TNF-α inhibitors**: The mainstay for refractory ocular Behçet's, particularly for posterior uveitis and retinal vasculitis.
- **Infliximab (Remicade)**: 5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6, then every 8 weeks. Rapid onset of action.
- **Adalimumab (Humira)**: 40 mg SC every 2 weeks. Convenient for long-term use.
- **Interferon-alpha (IFN-α)**: 3-9 million units SC three times weekly. Effective for ocular BD, especially for macular edema.
- **IL-1/IL-6 inhibitors**: Anakinra, Tocilizumab - emerging role for specific cases.
**4. Anticoagulation/Antiplatelet Therapy**: For specific vascular complications (e.g., DVT, cerebral venous thrombosis), but careful consideration due to aneurysm risk.
**5. Regular Monitoring**: Visual acuity, intraocular pressure, fundus exam, OCT, FFA, systemic disease activity, and side effects of medications.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques for Ocular Complications
content: Surgery for Behçet's complications carries a higher risk due to underlying inflammation and requires strict perioperative control of inflammation.
**Cataract Extraction**: Indicated for visually significant cataracts (common due to chronic inflammation and steroid use).
- Should be performed during periods of quiescent inflammation (minimum 3 months).
- Aggressive perioperative anti-inflammatory management with systemic and topical steroids is critical.
- Phacoemulsification with IOL implantation is standard.
**Vitrectomy**: Indicated for:
- Non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage.
- Tractional retinal detachment.
- Epiretinal membrane formation causing significant visual distortion/macular edema.
- Endophthalmitis (rare but possible complication).
**Glaucoma Surgery**: For secondary glaucoma refractory to medical management.
- Trabeculectomy with antimetabolites (MMC) or glaucoma drainage devices (e.g., Ahmed valve).
- High failure rate due to inflammation and scarring.
**Retinal Detachment Repair**: For rhegmatogenous or tractional retinal detachments. Requires meticulous technique and aggressive anti-inflammatory support.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Ocular Complications**:
- **Blindness**: Most feared complication, can be bilateral. Due to recurrent vasculitis, macular edema, optic atrophy, secondary glaucoma, complicated cataract, retinal detachment.
- Secondary glaucoma (neovascular or open-angle).
- Complicated cataract.
- Retinal detachment (rhegmatogenous, tractional, exudative).
- Vitreous hemorrhage.
- Epiretinal membrane, macular hole.
- Phthisis bulbi in end-stage severe disease.
**Systemic Complications**:
- Neurological damage (stroke, permanent disability from parenchymal lesions).
- Vascular thrombosis (DVT, pulmonary embolism, Budd-Chiari syndrome).
- Aneurysms (rupture can be fatal, e.g., pulmonary artery aneurysm).
- GI perforation, severe bleeding.
**Prognosis**:
- Chronic, relapsing-remitting course.
- Visual prognosis is guarded, especially with posterior segment involvement. Males, younger onset, and positive HLA-B51 associated with worse ocular prognosis.

- With modern immunosuppressive therapy, particularly biologics, prognosis for vision preservation has significantly improved. Systemic prognosis depends on vital organ involvement (CNS, large vessels).

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Sudden, severe vision loss or painful red eye**: Indicates active ocular inflammation (uveitis, vasculitis) requiring immediate aggressive immunosuppression.
**New-onset floaters, flashes, or curtain vision**: Suggests vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment.

**New neurological symptoms (headache, seizures, weakness, altered mental status)**: May indicate Neuro-Behçet's (meningoencephalitis, cerebral venous thrombosis) requiring urgent MRI and IV steroids.
**Severe, persistent headache with papilledema**: Signs of intracranial hypertension or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
**Sudden onset of abdominal pain with bleeding**: Potential GI ulcer perforation or hemorrhage.
**Unilateral limb swelling with pain (DVT)**: Sign of vascular thrombosis, requiring urgent workup and anticoagulation (with careful assessment for aneurysms first).
**Hemoptysis (coughing up blood)**: Potentially life-threatening pulmonary artery aneurysm rupture.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Recurrent hypopyon uveitis** is highly suggestive of Behçet's, especially in young males from endemic regions, even if other systemic features are initially absent.
**Pathergy test** is specific but not sensitive. A negative test does not rule out Behçet's, especially in non-endemic populations.
**Diagnosis is clinical**: No single diagnostic test; it relies on fulfilling the diagnostic criteria (e.g., ISG).
**Ocular Behçet's often leads to severe vision loss** without aggressive, early immunosuppression, frequently requiring systemic therapy (steroid-sparing agents and/or biologics).
**Posterior segment involvement (retinal vasculitis, optic neuropathy, macular edema)** carries a worse visual prognosis than isolated anterior uveitis.
**Male gender, younger age of onset, and HLA-B51 positivity** are often associated with more severe disease and worse visual outcomes.
**Close collaboration between ophthalmologists and rheumatologists** is crucial for optimal management of Behçet's Disease.
**Beware of masquerade syndromes**: Always rule out infectious etiologies (e.g., syphilis, TB) before initiating long-term immunosuppression.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Biologic Therapy**: Anti-TNF-α agents (Infliximab, Adalimumab) have revolutionized the treatment of refractory ocular Behçet's, significantly improving visual outcomes and reducing flare rates. (e.g., EURO-BEHCET study group trials).

**IL-6 and IL-1 Inhibition**: Emerging evidence supports the use of IL-6 inhibitors (Tocilizumab) and IL-1 inhibitors (Anakinra) for specific subsets of Behçet's patients, particularly those with CNS or severe vascular involvement refractory to anti-TNF-α.

**Genetic Research**: Ongoing studies continue to refine the understanding of genetic predisposition, beyond HLA-B51, identifying other risk alleles (e.g., in the IL-10 pathway, ERAP1) that contribute to disease susceptibility and phenotype.

**Improved Diagnostic Criteria**: The International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD), proposed in 2006 and revised, aims for better sensitivity and specificity compared to the ISG criteria, aiding earlier diagnosis.

**Imaging Biomarkers**: Advanced imaging techniques like OCT angiography and wide-field FFA are providing earlier detection and quantification of retinal vasculitis and related damage, guiding therapy and prognosis.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric Behçet's**: Rare, accounting for <5% of cases. Onset typically before 16 years. Diagnosis can be challenging due to non-specific symptoms and evolving criteria.
- Often presents with more severe disease and higher rates of neurological and vascular involvement compared to adults.
- Ocular involvement in children is frequently bilateral and severe, with high risk of blindness.
- Treatment generally follows adult guidelines but requires careful consideration of growth, development, and long-term side effects of immunosuppressants.

**Pregnancy**: Behçet's disease activity may fluctuate during pregnancy. Flare-ups (especially ocular) are possible. Careful management is needed, often involving systemic corticosteroids and select immunosuppressants (e.g., Azathioprine is generally considered safer than Mycophenolate Mofetil or Cyclophosphamide). Biologics like Infliximab/Adalimumab may be considered in severe cases after careful risk-benefit analysis.
**Elderly-onset Behçet's**: Rarer, often milder disease course. May have a lower incidence of ocular and neurological involvement. Diagnosis can be delayed due to confounding age-related conditions.
